title: TB8-07672
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (Appellant) is a citizen of Venezuela.

The Appellant fears Los Colectivos, a criminal group allied with the government, who threatened her and her family because they supported the opposition political party Primero Justicia. They killed her father on XXXX XXXX XXXX2017, and further threatened the remaining family members who were vocal about bringing them to justice.

The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) found the Appellant not to be credible because her mother omitted to mention in her support letter a threatening call received in February 2017; the Appellant's failure to recall the exact date of September 2017 when she received text threats; her failure to move after receiving the threatening text messages in September 2017, which suggested that her whereabouts were known; her 3-week delay in leaving Venezuela; and the lack of documentary evidence specifically from her sister to corroborate her allegations.

The Appellant essentially submits before the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) that the RPD erred in its appreciation of her mother's letter; failed to explain why she would be expected to recall the exact date of text messages beyond the month and year; failed to consider her explanation, her mental state and country conditions with regard to her delay in the departure; and failed to consider her explanation with regard to her failure to change residence, that she had nowhere else to go and that only the latest text messages suggested that her whereabouts were known. Furthermore, she argues that the RPD failed to assess her risk based on her profile and that there was no requirement for corroboration of facts by her sister. She submits one document for consideration as new evidence by the RAD.

I reject the document, which I do not find to be admissible. I agree with the Appellant that the RPD erred in the analysis of credibility, at times for reasons that differ from those raised by her, but mostly significantly because the RPD failed to assess her risk based on her strong political profile. I consider the evidence to be amply sufficient to render the correct decision, namely, that the Appellant has a well-founded fear of persecution on Convention grounds.
The appeal is allowed. I substitute my own decision that the Appellant is a Convention refugee.

According to the law,1 I can only accept evidence that: i. arose after the RPD decision; or ii. was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or that you could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before the decision.
If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible and relevant before I can accept it.2

The Appellant submits the March 2018 UNHCR, Guidance Note on the Outflow of Venezuelans, for consideration as new evidence. She explains that the document arose after the RPD decision and that the RAD should consider the most up-to-date information.

While I agree that this document arose after the RPD decision, it essentially contains evidence pertaining to ongoing facts which predate the decision already in evidence before the RPD. As such, the evidence it contains is not new and therefore I can not accept it.
My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.3

When considering this appeal, I took into consideration the Guidelines on Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution.4 The RPD erred when concluding that the Appellant's credibility was impugned by her mother's failure to mention the February 7, 2017, telephone threat specifically in her support letter.

The RPD states in its decision that it would have expected the February 7, 2017, telephone threat, the first against other family members other than the Appellant's father, to have been a major disruption to the family's sense of safety, making it sufficiently memorable to be included in the Appellant's mother's letter. It ultimately concludes that the February 7, 2017, threat did not take place as alleged, and that it was fabricated in an attempt to bolster the claim.

The Appellant, and to some extent the RPD, offer reasons pertaining to whether she or her mother's evidence ought to have been preferred. I do not find these arguments to be relevant as the two versions of events are not contradictory.

The Appellant's mother corroborates most of the events alleged in the claim. She specifically mentions that her husband received a telephone threat on January 28, 2017, but then adds, "...the threats over the phone continued, but this time addressed to him and the three of us..."

This in no way contradicts the Appellant's allegations and testimony that the threats started against her mother and her in the February 7th call. The two versions are absolutely compatible since February 7 is merely a few days and chronological after January 28. The fact that the date of February 7 is not mentioned specifically in the mother's letter is in no way a material omission considering the fact that it is referred to as having ensued after the January 28 call.

I agree with the Appellant that the RPD erred as it focussed on what the document did not say, and that she could not be expected to explain why the date of February 7 was not specifically mentioned since she is not the author of the letter. I find that the RPD erred when concluding that the Appellant's credibility was impugned by her mother's failure to mention the February 7, 2017, telephone threat specifically in her support letter. The RPD erred when concluding that the Appellant's credibility was impugned by the absence of further corroboration by way of a declaration by the Appellant's sister.

The error mentioned in the previous section is significant considering that it was an important credibility issue on which the RPD relied to conclude that the Appellant was never threatened by Los Colectivos and further to explain why, it considers that corroboration of the facts by the Appellant's sister would have been necessary.

Since I do not find that there actually was any contradiction or any significant omission, I also find that the RPD erred in concluding that the absence of further corroboration by way of a declaration by the Appellant's sister would have been necessary and impugns her credibility.

The fact that such a declaration would likely be available or usefully raised by the RPD is immaterial since there is a presumption of truth for testimony rendered under oath which is uncontradicted or disbelieved for valid reasons. Furthermore, I agree with the Appellant that the RPD erred as it failed to explain why the five other letters from various sources as well as pictures which corroborate almost every aspect of her claim would not suffice or be considered as credible. The RPD erred when drawing a negative inference regarding the Appellant's credibility because of her failure to recall the exact date of September 2017 text messages she received.

The RPD also made a negative finding regarding the Appellant's credibility as it found her testimony to be evasive regarding the date of September 2017 text messages. It stated that the Appellant did not know the date although she had specifically mentioned it in her Basis of Claim (BOC) form and had obtained copies of them recently.

The Appellant submits that a hearing before RPD is not "a memory test" and goes on to cite a number of Federal Court cases which found that it was unreasonable to expect the recollection of dates by asylum seekers.

I agree with the Appellant. As significant as these texts may have been, the RPD falls short of explaining why it would have expected a higher degree of precision than just the month and year which is nevertheless significantly precise for the purposes of the hearing.

In the absence of any further explanation, I find that the RPD erred when drawing a negative inference regarding the Appellant's credibility because of her failure to recall the exact date in September 2017 of text messages she received. The RPD erred as it failed to explain why the response given by the Appellant pertaining to why she did not move after receiving text messages on September 17, 2017, is not reasonable.

The RPD found that the actions of the Appellant further impugned her credibility. In particular, her failure to move after receiving threatening text messages in September 2017 which suggested that her whereabouts were known was a significant concern, as was her 3-week delay in leaving Venezuela after receiving these texts.

Concerning her failure to move, the Appellant submits that the RPD ignored the fact that sometime after the telephone threat of September 9, the family home in Cabimas was pelted with stones. Based on this, it was reasonable for the Appellant to believe, at that time, that the agents of persecution had not yet found her at her hiding location. She had also testified that she remained with her aunt and uncle because she did not have anywhere else to go. The RPD did not state why the Appellant's explanation that she had nowhere else to go was not a reasonable explanation.

The first argument has little merit since the RPD was clearly referring to that part of September after the 17th when the Appellant got a text citing by name the location where she was hiding at her uncle's house.

Nevertheless, I find that the argument that she had nowhere else to go has some value considering that she was a student who had suddenly and recently lost the support of her father due to an extraordinarily violent murder and that her uncle lived in a building that had a doorman. It is certainly not obvious on the face of the record that other options were available to her.

I conclude that the RPD did err as it failed to explain why the Appellant's answer is not satisfactory. The RPD erred when drawing a negative inference regarding the Appellant's credibility because of her 3-week delay in leaving Venezuela
The RPD drew a negative inference regarding the Appellant's credibility because of her 3-week delay in leaving Venezuela which she explained by XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX

The Appellant submits that an examination of the hearing recording reveals more precisely that she testified that XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXand then apply to come to Canada but, because of the situation that she and her family members found themselves in, she had to leave Venezuela sooner.
This argument does little more than to underline the fact that the question as to why she waited was not actually answered by the Appellant at the hearing.

The Appellant further argues that the RPD neglected to consider XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX to take the decision to flee her country permanently. In this instance, the RPD Member imposed his own individual expectations of what he would have done, or what he believes he would have done, had he been in the Appellant's position. Finally, she argues that she promptly departed Venezuela when one considers her personal limitations.

I find that the RPD did err when concluding that a 3-week delay in the departure would impugn the Appellant's credibility in her particular circumstances. The RPD erred when rejecting her claim without addressing this evidence pertaining to the strong political profile of the Appellant which establishes a well-founded prospective fear of persecution by Los Colectivos throughout Venezuela as well as the absence of state protection.

XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX were entered into the RPD record. Furthermore, the letter by her party confirms that she "is an active activist of the Primera Justicia party since April 2013, who has stood out as an advocate of our political ideals and for her continuous participation and cooperation in different activities..." (Emphasis added.) This evidence has not been contradicted.
I agree with the Appellant that the RPD erred when rejecting her claim without addressing this evidence pertaining to her profile.

Although I find no reason to doubt the credibility of the events alleged by the Appellant, I further find that this XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX would target her for persecution prospectively no matter where she might establish herself in Venezuela.

The objective evidence found in the NDP 5 confirms that Los Collectivos ruthlessly persecute political opposition activists throughout the country and that they act with total impunity and are actually supported by the government. Conclusion that the Appellant is credible well-founded fear of persecution

After examining the entire record, I find that all of the above suffices to find that the RPD erred when concluding that the Appellant is not credible. I am fully satisfied that that the Appellant is credible with regard to all of the essential elements of her claim and that she has a well-founded fear of persecution XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.

The appeal is allowed. I substitute my own decision that the Appellant is a Convention refugee.
